newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungarocamion boycotts Russia as trucks still held.
newsitem.headline: Hungarocamion boycotts Russia as trucks still held.

text.p: Central Europe's largest road haulage company Hungarocamion said the Hungarian transport minister's decision to write to Moscow to try secure the release of 19 impounded Hungarian trucks would not end its boycott of the country.
"We welcome the minister's concern but we don't think it will achieve very much -- Hungary's foreign and trade ministers should also help," Hungarocamion spokesman Gyorgy Rozsa told Reuters.
The company halted all deliveries to Russia last month following the seizure by Russian customs of five trucks. Four more had already been detained.

Hungarocamion used to carry up to half of all Hungary's road exports to Russia, while the former Soviet Union last year accounted for 15 percent of the company's annual turnover of 20 billion forints.
"We will not resume trade with Russia until we get the trucks back," sad Rozsa.

Transport minister Karoly Lotz said on Tuesday he would write to the Russian Minister of Transport and the head of the Russian Customs Committee to free 19 Hungarian trucks impounded in Russia since November. The 19 include nine Hungarocamion lorries worth a total $1.35 million.
Local customs headquarters seized the trucks claiming that duty had not been paid on the goods and intend to charge a storage fee of about USD 50 per day for each truck.
Hungarocamion claims all documents had been processed in advance according to TIR regulations.
Managing director Gabriella Szakall said earlier Russian customs officers commonly harassed drivers of Hungarian and Western trucks without apparent justification.
She said Russia had joined the TIR international transport agreement but had neglected to adjust internal regulations.

Rozsa said on Thursday Hungarocamion still had 50 trucks in Russia when it decided to stop operating there but had got them out by accepting Russian orders to transport goods to other parts of the former Soviet Union and then bringing the lorries back to Hungary via the Ukraine or Romania.
He added that the company had replaced the lost Russian business by finding alternative customers in Western Europe and former Yugoslavia but still wished to return to the large Russian market.
"We want to return to Russia but only if they will respect the legal way of doing things," he said.

Hungarocamion is due to be privatised later this year. The state privatisation agency APV said last month it would sell an 80 percent stake in the company, which has registered capital of 5.23 billion forints.
